A '''circular prime''' is a [[prime number]] with the property that the number generated at each intermediate step when cyclically permuting its (base 10) digits will be prime.<ref name="The Universal Book of Mathematics">{{Citation | publisher = Darling, David J. | title = The Universal Book of Mathematics | date = 11 August 2004 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=nnpChqstvg0C&dq=circular+prime&pg=PA70 | accessdate = 25 July 2010|page= 70| isbn = 9780471270478 }}</ref><ref name="Prime Numbers - The Most Mysterious Figures in Math">{{Citation | publisher = Wells, D. | title = Prime Numbers—The Most Mysterious Figures in Math | url = http://wenku.baidu.com/view/8d95d909581b6bd97f19ea85.html | accessdate = 27 July 2010|page=47 (page 28 of the book)}}</ref> For example, 1193 is a circular prime, since 1931, 9311 and 3119 all are also prime.<ref name="Circular primes">{{Citation | publisher = Patrick De Geest | title = Circular Primes | url = https://www.worldofnumbers.com/circular.htm | accessdate = 4 July 2025}}</ref>

A type of prime related to the circular primes are the [[permutable prime]]s, which are a subset of the circular primes (every permutable prime is also a circular prime, but not necessarily vice versa).<ref name="Circular primes" />

== Known circular primes ==

The first few circular primes are

:2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 31, 37, 71, 73, 79, 97, 113, 131, 197, 199, 311, 337, 373, 719, ... {{OEIS|id=A068652}}

The smallest representatives in each cycle of circular primes are

:2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 37, 79, 113, 197, 199, 337, 1193, 3779, 11939, 19937, 193939, 199933, R<sub>19</sub>, R<sub>23</sub>, ... {{OEIS|id=A016114}}

where R<sub>''n''</sub> := <math>\tfrac{10^n-1}{9}</math> is a [[repunit]], a number consisting only of ''n'' ones (in [[base 10]]). There are no other circular primes up to 10<sup>25</sup>.<ref name="Circular primes" />

The only other known examples are [[repunit prime]]s, which are circular primes by definition.

:R<sub>2</sub> (11), R<sub>19</sub>, R<sub>23</sub>, R<sub>317</sub>, R<sub>1031</sub>, R<sub>49081</sub>, R<sub>86453</sub>, R<sub>109297</sub>, R<sub>270343</sub>, R<sub>5794777</sub>, R<sub>8177207</sub>, ... {{OEIS|id=A004023}}

It is conjectured that there are only finitely many non-repunit circular primes.<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A293663}}</ref>

== Properties ==

A circular prime with at least two digits can only consist of combinations of the digits 1, 3, 7 or 9, because having 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 as the last digit makes the number divisible by 2, and having 0 or 5 as the last digit makes it divisible by 5.<ref name="The mathematics of Oz: mental gymnastics from beyond the edge">{{Citation | publisher = Pickover, Clifford A. | title = The mathematics of Oz: mental gymnastics from beyond the edge | date = 2 September 2002 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=4qA2qZhVb9AC&dq=circular+prime&pg=PA330 | accessdate = 9 March 2011|page=330| isbn = 9780521016780 }}</ref>

== Other bases ==

The complete listing of the smallest representative prime from all known cycles of circular primes in [[duodecimal|base 12]] is (using A and B for ten and eleven, respectively)
:2, 3, 5, 7, B, R<sub>2</sub>, 15, 57, 5B, R<sub>3</sub>, 117, 11B, 175, 1B7, 157B, 555B, R<sub>5</sub>, 115B77, R<sub>17</sub>, R<sub>81</sub>, R<sub>91</sub>, R<sub>225</sub>, R<sub>255</sub>, R<sub>4A5</sub>, R<sub>5777</sub>, R<sub>879B</sub>, R<sub>198B1</sub>, R<sub>23175</sub>, and R<sub>311407</sub>.

where R<sub>''n''</sub> is a repunit prime in base 12 with ''n'' digits. There are no other circular primes in base 12 up to 12<sup>12</sup>.

In [[binary number|base 2]], only [[Mersenne prime]]s can be circular primes, since any 0 permuted to the one's place results in an [[even number]].
